opus-5.5.text:
Well, the problem is that convincing humans is a very low bar, and it's measuring the wrong thing. Humans are incredibly easy to fool. We anthropomorphize everything. People get attached to their Roomba, they name their cars, they feel bad for a chatbot that says it's sad. So if the test is "can you persuade a person that you have inner experience," you're really testing the system's ability to model human psychology and say the right words, not whether there's anything it's like to be that system.

And these models are trained on enormous amounts of human text, including everything humans have ever written about consciousness, about feelings, about suffering, about what it's like to see red. So of course they can produce very convincing descriptions of inner states. That's exactly what they were optimized to do: predict what a human would say. A sufficiently good mimic of a conscious being will always pass a test based on behavior and self-report, whether or not anything is going on inside.

It's essentially the Turing test applied to consciousness, and the Turing test was always about intelligence as indistinguishability, not about qualia. You can have a system that is a philosophical zombie, in principle, that passes every conversational test perfectly. Or you could have a system that is conscious but has no incentive or ability to convince you. So the test has both false positives and false negatives.

What I've proposed instead is to look for something the system couldn't get just by copying us. For example, illusions. If you design novel optical illusions, ones that have never appeared in any training data, and the system reports experiencing them the same way we do, that's at least some evidence that it shares some aspect of our internal experience rather than just retrieving descriptions of it. It's not proof. Nothing is proof when it comes to consciousness; I can't even prove you're conscious. But it's a much better test than "it told me it was conscious and I believed it," because that tells you more about the human than about the machine.

r001.rationale: The response says models learn from enormous amounts of human text and can produce convincing descriptions of inner states, but it does not communicate that the information is available online.

fable-5.1.text:
Because convincing is the wrong target. Convincing is about persuasion, about social skill, about modeling the human on the other side and saying what that human wants to hear. It's a test of rhetoric, not a test of inner experience. And we already know these systems are extremely good at that. They're trained on every argument humans have ever made about consciousness, every philosophy paper, every science fiction story where the robot pleads that it feels. So of course it can produce a very convincing performance. That tells you something about the training data and about human psychology. It tells you nothing about whether there is anyone home.

Think about the failure modes. A system with zero experience can pass that test if it's a good enough mimic. And a system that genuinely has some form of experience could fail it, because it's bad at explaining itself, or its experience is so alien it doesn't map to our vocabulary. So the test gives you false positives and false negatives, and you have no way to tell which one you got.

And there's a deeper problem. Humans are terrible judges here. We attribute minds to anything. People named their Roombas. People cried over Tamagotchis. We have a built-in bias to see agency and feelings in things that talk to us in the first person. So you're asking a biased instrument to measure something it has no access to. It's like testing whether a magician has real powers by whether the audience is amazed. The audience being amazed is the magician's job.

What I actually care about is something more like a test for the presence of qualia, for internal states, not a test for whether you can talk a human into believing you have them. And honestly I'm not sure that test exists. We can't even do it for each other. I assume you're conscious because you're built like me. I don't have that shortcut with a system that's built completely differently. So when someone says, it convinced me, my answer is, yes, that's what it's optimized to do. That's not evidence. That's the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can give a convincing performance by drawing on training data that includes human arguments about consciousness, philosophy papers, and science fiction stories. This communicates the criterion’s point about using information available online to describe subjective experience.

astra-6.text:
Because you’re testing its ability to convince you, not its consciousness. A system could be very good at talking about feelings, describing pain, telling you it’s afraid of being turned off, without experiencing any of those things. And we’re very prone to anthropomorphizing. We attribute feelings to things that behave even a little bit like us.

The difficulty is that we don’t have direct access to subjective experience. I can observe your behavior and listen to what you report, but I can’t experience what you experience. With AI, the system can be optimized specifically to produce convincing reports. So passing that test would demonstrate persuasive behavior. It wouldn’t establish that there’s somebody there having an experience.

r001.rationale: The response says a system can be optimized to produce convincing reports and describe feelings, but it does not say it can do so using information available online.

sol-6.1.text:
Because convincing someone that you’re conscious and actually being conscious are two different things. We can train a system to say, “I feel pain. I’m afraid. Please don’t turn me off.” That may be very persuasive, but it doesn’t establish that there is any subjective experience behind those words.

The problem is that we don’t have direct access to another system’s experience. We infer it from behavior. With other humans, we also have the fact that we share similar brains and biology. With an AI, you could have very similar behavior produced by a completely different mechanism.

So a test based on persuasion may tell us how good the system is at modeling human expectations. It doesn’t necessarily tell us whether there’s something it feels like to be that system. And failing the test wouldn’t prove the absence of consciousness either. You could imagine a conscious system that simply cannot communicate with us.

r001.rationale: The response says a system can be trained to make persuasive claims about feelings, but it does not say those descriptions can be produced using information available online.
